newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Analysts side with S&P on Thailand ratings.
newsitem.headline: Analysts side with S&P on Thailand ratings.

text.p: Standard and Poor's more positive view on Thailand is closer to the mark than that of rival rating agency Moody's Investors Service, a panel of market experts said on Monday.

"S&P has it right and I think that the reason is because they have made a distinction between what is government risk and what is the risk in the financial sector," said John Sevilla, assistant director at Peregrine Fixed Income in Hong Kong
Sevilla was speaking on a Reuters Financial Television special report on Thailand.
Moody's on Friday said it might downgrade Thailand's A2 long-term foreign currency bond and deposit ratings. It also said it might cut the A2 senior ratings of five Thai banks.
The agency said that the review was prompted by concerns regarding the soundness of Thailand's financial sector as well as by constraints on macroeconomic policy-making.

S&P later said that it has no plans to cut Thailand's A2 long-term and A-1 short-term ratings because the country's economic fundamentals are strong enough to weather any crisis in the banking sector.
Sevilla said that while he remains cautious on Thailand's financial firms, "if you look at the sovereign risk per se, the government debt service is so small that it really is not at risk at all."
David Seto, senior country analyst at HSBC Markets, said that while weaker Thai banks could face further problems, he does not foresee shocks on a wider, systemic level.
He noted, for example, that Thailand's export performance, which was highlighted by Moody's as a source of concern, is expected to improve this year.

"It is important to remember that a lot of economists, including ourselves, have revised the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP (gross domestic product) downward relative to last year," said Seto, adding "that tells us that the worst of it is over on a systemic level."

Oliver Jory, head of debt capital markets at Morgan Stanley in Hong Kong, said the subdued reaction to the Moody's move in international debt markets demonstrates that foreign investors are still comfortable with Thai credits.
He said spreads on Thai paper traded in the U.S. market moved out just three to five basis points across the curve after widening a slightly greater amount in the previous few weeks.

"This widening of spreads is actually fairly muted in relation to the overall picture over the last six months, where we have seen a tightening of spreads," said Jory. He said recent weakness in Thai bonds is a buying opportunity.

While generally sanguine about Thailand's prospects, the panelists acknowledged that central bank efforts to defend the baht by raising interest rates could hinder economic recovery and weigh on the stock market.
"This type of strategy is quite dangerous to the local economy at the moment because...the Thai economy is not that strong," said Satian Tantanasarit, vice president and treasurer at Thai Danu Bank.
He said the Thai economy could withstand a short-term spike in rates of five to seven days, but a prolonged period of high interest rates would have damaging effects.
The panelists said they did not foresee a baht devaluation in the near-term.
They said the stock market outlook was poor for the next several months, but that the market should improve by year-end.
HSBC's Seto was said that while he expects a few more quarters of sluggishness in Thai stocks, "there is going to be an incredible rebound by the end of the year."
